pairs.evidence: app/_lib/python-runner.ts:602 On a timeout or abort, spawnPython SIGKILLs the Python child and then folds in only the ledger lines that were already written. A metered generation that was in flight at the kill gets no llm_usage row at all, and the ledger's outcome vocabulary has no 'indeterminate' value to record one. This is the technique's 'spend is real and unrecorded' case.

techniques.evidence: app/_lib/python-runner.ts:602 A killed metered generation is never closed: no synthetic row, no unknown-outcome status, and the spend goes unreconciled. The caller-facing half does conform: SpawnFailureKind at line 161 is a first-class kind rather than a message the caller has to parse.

app/_lib/llm-request-context.ts:54 Work the run owns (a companion turn running inside the digest task) inherits the outer run's id. A standalone companion turn names itself, and a spawn outside any scope inherits nothing (python-runner.ts:653 sets KP_LLM_REQUEST_ID only when a scope is open).

pairs.registryProposal: indeterminate-closure-on-interruption covers restart recovery and runtime-held calls. It does not name the case where the host deliberately kills a metering subprocess on timeout or abort, and the child's ledger write dies with it. That is the commonest way a metered generation goes unrecorded in a spawn-per-request runtime, and the fix there is a parent-side synthetic row.

pairs.evidence: app/api/devcase/session/[id]/chat/route.ts:105 The candidate's message is stored before the generation, and the only thing that closes it is a successful reply (line 133). An abort, timeout or crash leaves an unanswered user turn with no status saying the outcome is unknown. Both later readers then trip over that gap: the next turn feeds it to the model through getDevSessionChat, and the evaluator reads the captured prompt channel as evidence.
